answers.text: The brief only says 'managed secret store' and does not name the product, its CLI or its read call. I added an assumption saying what 'store CLI' and 'latest version' mean (newest version returned when no version id is given; every write makes a new id, per the brief) and an open question to confirm the product and call before step 9.

deploy.md checks out that all 4 prod replicas run under the service identity orders-api-prod, and step 1 gives that identity read-only on orders-api/prod/*. How the platform attaches the identity to a pod is not in the brief or the files. Added to assumptions and open questions.

APP_ENV is set by each environment's deployment manifest (prod for the prod deployment); no existing file defines it, so this is my design choice. A wrong value cannot yield a wrong key: orders-api-prod is denied on non-prod paths (step 1 negative test), so the pod exits at startup. Added to step 3.

Yes, if any one read fails the whole attempt fails and all three are re-read next time; that is the simplest rule. The 3 s timeout covers a whole attempt and the 2 s wait comes after each failed attempt, so the old '6 s' was wrong: worst case is 4x3 + 3x2 = 18 s. Fixed in steps 3 and 12.
The previous value is kept per secret until that same secret's next swap, which replaces it. There is no timer, because a timer is an extra mechanism the brief does not require. Added to step 6.

The old wording 'changed in the last refresh' was vague. Now: the fallback applies per secret whenever that secret has a previous value, which stays until that secret's next swap. The client needs no extra flag. Reworded in step 7.

No conflict. Per deploy.md the image includes config/app.yaml as in the repo, so an old pod has the old code and old yaml together and never runs the new loader. The new image has a yaml with no api_key, so the new guard passes. The guard checks only its own image's yaml. Clarified in step 12.

No sticky switch: every call tries the current value first, and only retries once with the previous value after a 401/403, logging a warning each time. Simpler than tracking state. If both are rejected, the call returns the provider's error as today, and the fix is a corrected store write picked up within 5 minutes. Clarified in step 7.

questions.text: Where do the 'previous' value and the current value come from at startup, and after a pod restarts mid-rotation? Is the previous value empty after any restart, so the 401 fallback only works after a pod has seen two swaps?
questions.about: Step 6 Refresh every 5 minutes / Step 7 Bad new value

questions.text: The fallback only applies when a secret has a previous value. When a new key is first rotated in, what is the 'previous' value: the old key from the store, or something else? At the first migration, the old key is in yaml, not in the store, so what does a new pod have as previous?
questions.about: Step 7 Bad new value / Step 12 Merge and deploy

questions.text: The refresh thread reads 'the latest version' of each secret. If a secret write is made wrongly (a mistyped value), who notices it and how? What triggers the corrected write?
questions.about: Step 7 Failure handling after startup: If it fails

questions.about: Step 7 Repeated failure

questions.about: Step 1 Create the paths and access rules / Step 2 Rotate

questions.about: Step 5 Using a key on each request / holder

questions.text: Step 11 says a developer's make run uses fixed fake keys in config/app.local.yaml, but step 3 says the loader refuses to start if config/app.yaml contains any api_key. How do local mode and the loader guard fit together, and does the local mode use the secrets module at all?
questions.about: Step 11 Local development / Step 3 Startup load

answers.text: At startup the current value is the store's newest version and the previous value is empty. After a restart it is empty again, so the 401 fallback exists only after a pod has seen a swap. I kept this because loading older versions is an extra mechanism the brief does not require. Stated in steps 3, 6 and 7.

At the first migration a new pod has no previous value. The old key lives only in the old image's yaml, not in the store. The protection there is the step 2 test call on each new key before it is written, plus both keys staying active and rollback to the old image. Stated in step 7.

A mistyped write is caught first by the step 2 test call. If it still gets through, it shows up in the step 13 error-rate check and in the fallback warnings in the logs. The security on-call engineer makes the corrected write, and pods pick it up within 5 minutes. Added to step 7. No new alert for fallback warnings: the brief does not require one.

The brief and files do not name an alerting system or a recipient. I assume a rule on the central log service, because that is the only monitoring source in deploy.md, but this is not confirmed. Added to step 7 and to Open questions.

deploy.md says deploys are rolling, one pod at a time, with maxUnavailable: 0, and that a new pod must pass its readiness probe (GET /healthz returns 200) before an old pod stops. So yes, the platform calls /healthz. It does not say which file holds the maxUnavailable setting, only that it is the deployment's rolling-update config. Clarified in step 4.

The store CLI writes the secret value to the named path and prints the new version id. The security on-call engineer runs it under their own identity, which gets write through membership of the security on-call group. That is a different identity from orders-api-prod. How membership is granted is not in the brief, so I left it to security. Added to the assumptions and step 2.

A call reads the value once when it builds its header, so a mid-request swap does not affect that call. Either value is valid during a rotation. The lock only stops a reader from seeing a new value paired with an old version id (or the reverse). Added to step 5.

This was a real conflict, and I changed the plan. The guard and the CI check both flag api_key, so fake keys under api_key in the local file would fail them. Now the local file keeps fake keys under a local_secrets section, and the secrets module reads that section when APP_ENV=local, with no store call. The holder, the clients and the guard behave the same in every mode. Changed steps 3 and 11.

questions.about: Step 11 Local development

answers.text: No, it accepts whatever the store returns as newest. Checking a value would need a provider call from the refresh thread, an extra mechanism the brief does not require. The protections are the step 2 test call before the write and the step 7 401/403 fallback after it. Stated in step 6.

The security on-call engineer does it by hand: lists pods from the cluster, reads each pod's latest refresh line in the central logs, and compares the version ids with the store's current versions via the store CLI, then records the result in the ticket. Automating it is not required by the brief. Stated in step 15.

Running pods keep their values in memory, so a store outage does not stop them. In a rolling deploy, new pods never turn ready and the old pods keep serving (maxUnavailable 0, per deploy.md). A pod that crashes and restarts during the outage cannot come back until the store returns; I accept that as the simplest rule since the brief requires exit after retries. Added to step 3.

Nothing is affected. Per deploy.md the old image bakes in the old config/app.yaml and old code, which never read the store, and the old key stays active at the provider. Added a line to steps 2 and 12.

Yes, dev goes through the same secrets code as prod: same startup retries, readiness and refresh thread, just reading orders-api/dev/* under the developer's identity. Only APP_ENV=local skips the store. Stated in step 11.

questions.text: When the security engineer writes a new version of a secret, what exactly makes the refresh thread see it as 'changed'? Is it just a different version id from the one in the holder?
questions.about: Step 6 Refresh every 5 minutes

questions.text: The refresh thread starts after startup. Does it start only after all three secrets load, and does it run on every pod independently, so pods may swap at different moments within the 5 minutes?
questions.about: Step 6 Refresh every 5 minutes

questions.text: In the first migration, new pods use the new key from the store and old pods use the old key. At which point in the rollout does a new pod first make a real provider call with the new key, and what shows that the key works before it takes traffic?
questions.about: Step 12 Merge and deploy

questions.text: The fallback retry on 401/403 resends the call with the previous value. What if the provider answers 403 for a reason unrelated to the key (for example a permission or business rule)? Does the retry still happen?
questions.about: Step 7 Bad new value

questions.text: What does the exit code of the process cause on the platform when startup load fails? Does the restarted pod retry the whole 18 s sequence again, and how long until someone is told the rollout is stuck?
questions.about: Step 3 Startup load: If it fails

questions.text: Where are the deploy.md rollback and the 'refuse images built before the migration image' rule enforced, and what is 'deploy tooling' here?
questions.about: Step 14 Close the rollback hole

answers.text: Yes. A secret counts as changed when the version id the store returns differs from the version id held in memory. Simplest rule, and the brief guarantees every write gets a new version id. Stated in step 6.

The refresh timer starts only after the startup load has succeeded, which is also what readiness requires. Each pod runs its own independent timer, so pods swap at different moments within 5 minutes of a new write. That is fine because both old and new values are valid during a rotation. Stated in step 6.

A new pod makes its first provider call on the first customer request it serves after turning ready. Nothing checks the key between load and that request, because readiness only proves the keys loaded; a provider call in the probe would be an extra mechanism the brief does not require. The protection is the step 2 test call before the write, the step 13 error-rate check, rollback, and the old key staying active. Stated in steps 4 and 12.

The client cannot tell a key-related 403 from an unrelated one, so the retry happens in both cases, costing one extra call. If the retry is also rejected, the call returns the provider's answer to the current value, as today. Retrying is safe because a refused call was not processed. Stated in step 7.

The plan assumes the platform restarts the container, and that the restarted process runs the whole 18 s sequence again. For a rolling deploy, deploy.md only says the rollout halts and old pods keep serving. It does not say how the platform backs off between restarts, how long until a stuck rollout is noticed, or who is told. I did not invent an alert; the person running the deploy watches rollout status. Added to step 3, step 12 and the open questions.

deploy.md does not name the deploy tooling or where rollbacks are enforced; it only says rollback is redeploying an earlier image. 'Deploy tooling' here means whatever system performs those redeploys, and where the refuse-old-images rule can be configured is unconfirmed. Added a definition in step 14 and an open question to confirm before step 14.

teachbacks.text:
1. Before anything else, security/platform creates two store paths, `orders-api/prod/*` and `orders-api/dev/*`. Each has its own KMS key, and audit logging is on for reads and writes. The service identity `orders-api-prod` gets read-only on prod. The security on-call group gets write on prod. Engineers get read on dev only. Four access tests must pass before any secret is written: an engineer is denied prod, `orders-api-prod` is denied a write, `orders-api-prod` is denied dev, and `orders-api-prod` can read prod. If one is wrong, the policy is fixed and the tests are re-run. The app is untouched at this point, so nothing is at risk.

2. A security on-call engineer creates a new key at each provider (payments, email, geocoding) while the old key stays active. They make one test call per new key. They write each value into `orders-api/prod/<name>` with the store CLI under their own identity. Every write creates a new version id, and only the version ids go in the rollout ticket. A key that fails its test call is deleted and replaced. A failed write is retried. Existing pods never read the store, so nothing changes for them.

3. One PR adds the `secrets` module and changes the three clients and `/healthz`. It deletes the `api_key` lines from `config/app.yaml`. It adds a loader guard that refuses to start if the loaded file contains an `api_key`. It also adds a CI guard that fails on an `api_key` key or on `pk_live_`/`ml_live_`/`geo_live_` strings, and that guard is a required check on `main`. Tests must pass before merge. They cover the retry and exit behaviour, last-good retention, 503 until loaded, use of a new value without a restart, the 401 fallback, and a canary test that a secret never appears in logs, `os.environ` or files.

4. The PR is merged and CI builds an image with no keys. The rolling deploy (`maxUnavailable: 0`) starts one new pod at a time. An old pod is stopped only after a new pod's `GET /healthz` probe returns 200. Old pods keep using the old key from their baked-in yaml. New pods use the new key from the store. Both keys are active, so calls succeed either way.

5. Startup load, in each new pod. The pod's `APP_ENV` selects the path `orders-api/<APP_ENV>/<name>`. With `local` there is no store call, and the holder is filled from `local_secrets` in `config/app.local.yaml`. In other environments the pod reads all three secrets using its service identity. No store credential is in the image or environment. Non-secret settings still come from `config/app.yaml` via `config_loader.py`. The holder keeps each secret's value, version id and previous value (empty at startup). It swaps under a lock, so the value and version id always match. A wrong `APP_ENV` in prod means a denied read, so the pod exits.

6. Startup retries. Each attempt reads all three secrets with a timeout of about 3 s. If any read fails, the whole attempt fails, and the pod waits 2 s before the next one. There are 4 attempts in total, so the worst case is 18 s. After the 4th failure the pod logs the error (no values) and exits non-zero (for example 3). The platform is expected to restart it. "Denied" and "not found" are treated the same as other failures. During a rollout this pod never turns ready, so the rollout halts and the old pods keep serving. Recovery is to fix the policy or roll back to the earlier image, which still works because the old key is active.

7. Readiness. The platform calls `/healthz`. It returns 503 until all three secrets are loaded (the holder's "all loaded" flag), then 200 `{"status": "ok"}`. Other routes also return 503 while the holder is empty. Readiness proves only that the keys loaded. It makes no provider call. Once the probe returns 200, an old pod is stopped and the next pod is replaced. This repeats until all 4 pods are new.

8. A customer request needing a provider call. The client calls `secrets.get("payments_api_key")` (or the email or geocoding equivalent) and builds the `Authorization` header from that value. It reads the value once per call. The clients do not copy the key at construction, so a refreshed key is used on the next call without a restart. The header lives only for that request. If the holder is somehow empty, the request returns 503 and the secret name is logged. A new pod's first use of its key is the first customer request after it turns ready. Nothing checks it before then.

9. Refresh. After a successful startup load, a background timer fires every 5 minutes. Each pod has its own timer, so pods pick up a new write at different moments within 5 minutes. The refresh reads the latest version of each secret. A secret counts as changed when its version id differs from the holder's. For each changed secret the new value is swapped in, and the replaced value becomes that secret's previous value. That previous value lasts until the next swap of that secret, or until a restart empties it. The new value is not validated. The refresh logs one info line per cycle with version ids only, for example `secrets refreshed payments=v7 email=v3 geocoding=v4`. Logs are kept 30 days.

10. Failures after startup. If a refresh read fails, the pod keeps the last good value, logs a warning (secret name and error, no values) and retries at the next tick. Refresh failures never change readiness. Three failed cycles in a row (15 minutes) should raise an alert, assumed to be a rule on the central logs. If a provider returns 401 or 403 for the current key, the client retries that call once with the previous value, if one exists, and logs a warning. It does not switch permanently. It retries on any 403, because it cannot tell a key-related 403 from an unrelated one. If the retry is also rejected, the provider's answer to the current value is returned. A freshly started pod has no previous value, so it has no fallback. The pre-write test call in step 2 is what protects that case. A bad write is handled by the security on-call making a corrected write, which every pod picks up within 5 minutes.

11. Verify and soak. Once all 4 pods are on the new image, check that each pod has a startup line and a refresh line with the expected version ids. Check that error and latency rates for payments, email and geocoding match the baseline. Soak for at least 1 hour and at least 3 clean refresh cycles. If something is wrong, roll back to the earlier image, or correct the store value.

12. Before revoking the old keys, deploy tooling is configured to refuse any image built before the migration image, because those images hold the old keys. Each provider's usage or audit view is used to find who still calls with the old keys. Expected callers are developers' `make run` and old pods that are gone by now. Engineers are told that old local checkouts will stop working. An unknown caller, or no way to see usage, holds the revocation until security accepts the risk in writing.

13. Revocation. This needs the security on-call engineer's explicit sign-off. The evidence is collected by hand and recorded in the ticket. The cluster lists exactly the expected pods, all on the migration image or later. Each pod's latest refresh line matches the store's current versions. No refresh alert is open. The old key has not been used since the final pod switched, where the provider shows last use. Revocation goes one provider at a time (geocoding, then email, then payments). A reversible "disable" comes first if offered, then 15 minutes of watching error rates, then delete. If errors appear after a disable, the old key is re-enabled. If it can't be re-enabled, another key is issued and written to the store, and the refresh delivers it.

14. Close out. Confirm the CI guard is required on `main`, and that `deploy.md` describes the store, the 5-minute refresh and the local modes. Record the final version ids and revocation dates. Git history is not rewritten, because the keys in it are dead.

15. Local development. `make run` uses `APP_ENV=local`, with `config/app.local.yaml` pointing `base_url` at the stubs from `make stubs`. The fake keys in `local_secrets` fill the holder, and there is no store call. `make run-sandbox` sets `APP_ENV=dev`. It reads `orders-api/dev/*` under the developer's own identity and uses the same secrets code as prod. If the sandbox read is denied, it falls back to the stubs.

16. Later rotations use the same mechanism. Issue a new key, test it, write it to the store, and wait at least 2 refresh cycles (10 minutes). Then confirm every pod shows the new version id, and revoke the old key.
gaps: The store product and its read call are not named, so I cannot say what call a pod actually makes or how the store checks the pod's identity.
I cannot say how the platform attaches the `orders-api-prod` identity to a pod, which the startup read depends on.
The system that raises the three-failed-cycles refresh alert, and who receives it, is unknown.
I do not know how the platform restarts a container that exited, including any backoff, or how soon anyone notices a stuck rollout or who is told.
The deploy tooling is not named, so I cannot say where the 'refuse images built before the migration image' rule is configured or whether it can be.
